Direct or close exposure to any animal with bird flu is a [...] Very rarely, limited spread of an avian influenza A virus has occurred in other countries from a sick person to another person who was not wearing recommended protective equipment. This has occurred in other countries after prolonged close exposure, such as when one family member was providing care for another family member who was very sick from avian influenza A virus infection.

title: Bird flu has devastated wildlife around the world. What Australian birds are most at risk? - The Guardian
snippet: It’s uncertain how native populations might be affected by the deadly H5 strain but seagulls, pelicans and black swans are among those species that have experts worried. The federal government announced the first vaccination plans for captive native bird species last week and the Victorian government has moved to vaccinate wild little penguins after the first detections in terns on Phillip Island. On Saturday, the state government announced the death of a little penguin on the island, the first confirmed case of H5 bird flu in the species. But for those who don’t live in communities in southern Australia on the frontline of the highly pathogenic virus, the possibility that they will at some point see the severe consequences of H5 bird flu for native birds might not have registered. There is a level of uncertainty about how native species will be affected as they are exposed to the deadly strain for the first time. Here are the birds experts are most concerned about – including some of Australia’s most common and loved species.

title: Australia has just 12,000 sea lions left – and ‘carnage’ may await them as bird flu takes hold, scientists warn - The Guardian
snippet: Scientists have warned deadly H5 bird flu could cause “carnage” for Australia’s seal and sea lion populations after detection of the virus in long-nosed fur seals in South Australia. SA confirmed Australia’s first case in a mammal on Saturday after a dead long-nosed fur seal found at Beachport on the Limestone Coast tested positive for H5N1. “It’s likely in the next few weeks it will spread more quickly into the sea lion population in South Australia generally because of the proximity of the sea lion colonies to breeding seabird colonies or affected seabirds.”. H5 bird flu has already affected pinnipeds in South America and sub-Antarctica, where it has caused catastrophic losses in populations of some species, particularly among pups. “With reported mass mortality of terns and now the death of a long-nosed fur seal on the Pages it is now highly likely that this vital population of Australian sea lions has also been exposed to the virus,” she said.

title: Thousands of baby seals died on two remote sub-Antarctic islands. Scientists now think they know why - CNN
snippet: Drone surveys conducted by the Australian Antarctic Program in October and January revealed “sobering” images of seal pup carcasses littering the grayish volcanic shores of Heard and McDonald Islands, Jarrod Hodgson, a senior research scientist at the organization said. The southern elephant seal pup mortality was estimated to be 76% across a population of 17,000 seal pups born on the islands, the program said. “The thing we don’t know from our surveys so far is what the impact was on the breeding adult population of southern elephant seals,” Hodgson said. “These observations of H5 bird flu at Heard Island and McDonald Island are the first detection in an Australian external territory and show the continued eastward movement of the virus around the sub-Antarctic,” wildlife biologist Julie McInnes said. Wildlife experts assessed a H5 bird flu mass mortality event among southern elephant seals at Capsize Beach, Paddick area of Heard Island, Australia on October 2025.

title: Fears for ‘gregarious’ local celebrity Sammy the elephant seal in Victorian bird flu hotspot - The Guardian
snippet: # Fears for ‘gregarious’ local celebrity Sammy the elephant seal in Victorian bird flu hotspot. Seals and sea lions often communicate by touch and share spaces with wild birds, placing them at risk of infection from H5N1 virus. Since H5 bird flu arrived in Portland, Victoria, the situation has been “pretty grim” with many dead and suffering birds on the beach, and the dilemma of how to dispose of the carcasses, according to local resident Lynn Murrell. But since the first confirmed case in a fur seal on Sunday at Beachport, South Australia – a two-hour trip over the border – people have been worried for their local “pet seal”, known as Sammy. Victoria’s first bird flu case was detected in the town, in the far south-west of the state, at the end of July. Seals and sea lions often share spaces with wild birds, placing them at risk of infection from H5 bird flu.

title: ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed - theguardian.com
snippet: # ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed. As Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impacts. It’s only been three weeks since H5 bird flu was detected on South Australia’s Limestone Coast, and already encounters with sick or dead birds are becoming commonplace. “We expected it, but now it’s here, it’s just traumatic.”. Since the first case in a local Australian seabird – a greater crested tern – was detected in early July, the region has seen dozens more suspected and confirmed cases, including the first confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks, a group of islets about 8km from the coastal town of Robe. As the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, observed on Monday, the events rapidly unfolding in the south-east, and around Australia, are “the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife.”.

title: Vietnam remains on alert for emerging avian influenza variants
snippet:
In Vietnam, amid the impacts of climate change and the increasing overlap of migratory bird flyways, avian influenza outbreaks are becoming more complex and unpredictable. Similar trends are also being observed in many other countries.

The continuous evolution of influenza viruses and the emergence of new variants require poultry producers and industry stakeholders to remain highly vigilant.

Rising threat from highly pathogenic avian influenza strains [...] Since the beginning of the year, sporadic outbreaks have been reported in several provinces, including Ha Tinh, Ninh Binh, and Dien Bien. These incidents have resulted in significant economic losses and forced authorities to cull large numbers of poultry to prevent further spread of the disease.

In response, the Vietnamese Government has approved the National Avian Influenza Prevention and Control Plan for the 2026-2030 period, with key targets including:

Continue after advertising. [...] Reducing the number of outbreaks by at least 30% compared with the average recorded during 2019–2025.

Avian flu — which, in another, milder strain is much like the common cold in wild birds — morphed and became pathogenic when chickens and other poultry at industrial-scale producers were exposed to the virus through contact with migrating flocks of wild birds. Since it first appeared in Europe in 2020, this “Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza” strain has devastated wildlife worldwide, the largest avian flu outbreak ever. And this panzootic is obviously not over. [...] Some of the wildlife victims are endangered species, and this virus’s ability to spread to new hosts is astounding. As of December 2025, H5N1 had infected some 598 types of bird and 102 mammal species, according to the United Nations. The numbers have jumped substantially over the past 18 months: As of August 2024, the U.N. tally was 485 bird and 48 mammal species.

snippet:
# H5N1 outbreaks hit more commercial poultry in 3 states

News brief

Lisa Schnirring

Avian Influenza (Bird Flu)

Copied to clipboard

A trio of Midwestern states—Iowa, Minnesota, and Wisconsin—reported new H5N1 avian flu outbreaks in poultry on commercial farms, according to notifications from state agencies.

 turkey flock 

Myles Tan / Flickr cc [...] Meanwhile, the Minnesota Board of Animal Health (MBAH) added two new H5N1 poultry outbreaks to its notification list, one in Becker County and the other in Otter Tail County. The two counties neighbor each other in the state’s west central region. Both are breeder poultry farms, and together the facilities house more than 36,000 birds.

Minnesota has now recorded eight outbreaks in poultry since the middle of September, part of a national rise in activity. [...] The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship (IDALS) said it and the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) have detected H5N1 on a commercial turkey farm in Calhoun County in the west central part of the state.

Officials said the outbreak is Iowa’s eighth in domestic birds this year. The state reported its last poultry outbreak in April.
